questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: The most common carcinoma of the pancreas is:
questions.exp: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: m/c carcinoma of pancreas. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Which of the following is a risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
questions.exp: Risk factors: smoking, obesity, African American ethnicity, genetic factors, chronic pancreatitis, syndromes. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Which of the following is a risk factor for pancreatic cancer?
questions.exp: Risk factors: African American ethnicity. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: The PRSS1 gene is associated with which pancreatic condition as a risk factor for cancer?
questions.exp: Genetic factors: PRSS1 gene — hereditary pancreatitis. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: The SPINK1 gene is associated with:
questions.exp: Genetic factors: SPINK1 gene — tropical calcific pancreatitis. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Which syndrome raises the risk of pancreatic cancer by 100 folds?
questions.exp: Syndromes: STK11 Peutz-Jeghers syndrome — risk of pancreatic cancer raised by 100 folds. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Which of the following is a syndrome listed as a risk factor for pancreatic cancer?
opts: Familial atypical mole and multiple melanoma syndrome
questions.exp: Syndromes: familial atypical mole and multiple melanoma syndrome, cystic fibrosis, BRCA-2 gene mutation, Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Familial adenomatous polyposis raises the risk of:
opts: Periampullary cancer and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
questions.exp: Syndromes: familial adenomatous polyposis — risk of periampullary cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: The BRCA-2 gene predisposes to which combination of cancers?
opts: Pancreatic, prostate and male breast cancer
questions.exp: Note: BRCA-2 gene predisposes to pancreatic, prostate, male breast cancer. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: Lynch syndrome raises the risk of:
questions.exp: Note: Lynch — raised risk of colorectal cancer. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: PanIN stands for:
questions.exp: PanIN: pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: In the PanIN sequence, the first and most common mutation is:
questions.exp: PanIN diagram: PanIN-1A/1B — K-ras, 1st and m/c mutation. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: In the PanIN sequence, the mutation seen at PanIN-2A is:
questions.exp: PanIN diagram: PanIN-2A — CDKN2A. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: In the PanIN sequence, PanIN-3 carries which mutations before the final hit?
questions.exp: PanIN diagram: PanIN-3 — p53, SMAD4, then final hit. (Book p297)

questions.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
questions.q: The mnemonic for the pancreatic cancer mutation sequence (K-ras, p53, SMAD4) is:
questions.exp: Mnemonic: K53. (Book p297)

questions.q: Periampullary carcinoma is a group of how many cancers within 2 cm of the ampullary opening?
questions.exp: Periampullary carcinoma: group of 4 cancers within 2 cm of ampullary opening. (Book p298)

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four periampullary cancers?
questions.exp: Periampullary: 1. Carcinoma head of pancreas, 2. Ampullary variety, 3. Cholangiocarcinoma of distal CBD, 4. Duodenal adenocarcinoma. (Book p298)

questions.q: The four periampullary cancers share:
questions.exp: Periampullary carcinoma: similar presentation and Mx. (Book p298)

questions.q: The most common presentation of periampullary carcinoma is:
opts: Progressive obstructive jaundice due to CBD obstruction
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: progressive obstructive jaundice d/t CBD obstruction — m/c presentation. (Book p298)

questions.q: Obstructive jaundice from a periampullary tumour is also called:
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: aka surgical jaundice. (Book p298)

questions.q: Pain in pancreatic carcinoma is of high intensity when the tumour is in the:
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: pain — high intensity in tail and body. (Book p298)

questions.q: Waxing and waning jaundice is a specific presentation of:
questions.exp: Specific presentations: waxing and waning of jaundice — seen in ampullary variety. (Book p298)

questions.q: In waxing jaundice of an ampullary tumour, the fall in jaundice is associated with:
questions.exp: Waxing and waning: decreased jaundice — associated with melena (friable tumour growth obstructs bile, then sloughs off, causing decreased jaundice and melena). (Book p298)

questions.q: Gastric outlet obstruction with jaundice is a specific presentation of:
questions.exp: Specific presentations: gastric outlet obstruction — seen in duodenal adenocarcinoma, associated with jaundice. (Book p298)

questions.q: Courvoisier's law states that obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder is:
opts: Always due to a Phrygian cap
questions.exp: Courvoisier's law: obstructive jaundice + palpable gallbladder — seldom d/t stone disease. (Book p298)

questions.q: A tumour blocking the CBD produces:
opts: A dilated biliary tree and a distended, palpable, pyriform gallbladder
questions.exp: Courvoisier's law: tumour blocking CBD — obstruction, dilated biliary tree, distended gallbladder (palpable, pyriform shaped). (Book p298)

questions.q: In gall stone obstruction of the CBD, the gallbladder does NOT distend because of:
questions.exp: Courvoisier's law: gall stones causing obstruction of CBD — no distension of GB d/t inflammatory fibrosis of gallbladder; jaundice plus shrunken gallbladder. (Book p298)

questions.q: An exception to Courvoisier's law is:
questions.exp: Exceptions: primary CBD stones (10% cases). (Book p299)

questions.q: Which of the following is an exception to Courvoisier's law?
questions.exp: Exceptions: double impaction of stone, oriental cholangiohepatitis, Mirizzi syndrome. (Book p299)

questions.q: Oriental cholangiohepatitis, an exception to Courvoisier's law, is due to infection by:
questions.exp: Exceptions: oriental cholangiohepatitis — d/t infection by Chinese liver fluke. (Book p299)

questions.q: Mirizzi syndrome, an exception to Courvoisier's law, involves:
opts: A fistula between the gallbladder and the CBD
questions.exp: Exceptions: Mirizzi syndrome — fistula between gallbladder and CBD. (Book p299)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for pancreatic carcinoma is:
questions.exp: Investigation: CECT — IOC. (Book p299)

questions.q: Duodenography in pancreatic carcinoma shows:
questions.exp: Duodenography: Frostberg reverse 3 sign. (Book p299)

questions.q: Duodenography for pancreatic carcinoma is:
questions.exp: Duodenography: obsolete. (Book p299)

questions.q: The X-ray finding in pancreatic carcinoma is:
questions.exp: X-ray: widening of duodenal loops. (Book p299)

questions.q: The double duct sign on MRCP/ERCP means:
opts: Blockage of the ampullary opening with widening of the pancreatic duct and CBD
questions.exp: MRCP, ERCP — double duct sign: blockage of ampullary opening, widening of pancreatic duct and CBD. (Book p299)

questions.q: When the radiological diagnosis of a pancreatic head mass is in doubt, the next step is:
questions.exp: Radiological diagnosis, in doubt — trans gastric EUS guided FNAC (EUS — endoscopic guided ultrasound). (Book p299)

questions.q: CA 19-9 in pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: CA 19-9: predictive and prognostic marker. (Book p299)

questions.q: CA 19-9 helps identify patients for:
questions.exp: CA 19-9: identifies patients for staging laparoscopy — done prior to definitive Sx in GI tumors to identify metastases. (Book p299)

questions.q: A raised CA 19-9 is an indication for:
questions.exp: CA 19-9: raised CA 19-9 — indication for staging laparoscopy. (Book p299)

questions.q: A normal CA 19-9 after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is:
questions.exp: CA 19-9 (normal) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy — important prognostic marker (not specific). (Book p299)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions shows a raised CA 19-9?
questions.exp: Conditions with raised CA 19-9: cholangio-carcinoma, gall bladder cancer, pancreatic cancer. (Book p299)

questions.q: Staging of pancreatic cancer uses PET CT, which stands for:
questions.exp: Staging: PET CT — positron emitted tomography. (Book p299)

questions.q: In the AJCC classification (7th and 8th editions), T1 pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: AJCC: T1 — diameter ≤2 cm. (Book p300)

questions.q: T2 pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: AJCC: T2 — diameter 2-4 cm. (Book p300)

questions.q: T3 pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: AJCC: T3 — diameter >4 cm. (Book p300)

questions.q: T4 pancreatic cancer is defined by:
questions.exp: AJCC: T4 — adjacent structure involvement. (Book p300)

questions.q: The most common site of distant metastasis (M1) in pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: Metastasis staging: M1 — distant metastasis, m/c site — liver. (Book p300)

questions.q: In nodal staging, N1 pancreatic cancer means:
questions.exp: Nodal staging: N0 — no regional nodes, N1 — 1-3 regional nodes, N2 — >3 regional nodes. (Book p300)

questions.q: In nodal staging, N2 pancreatic cancer means:
questions.exp: Nodal staging: N2 — >3 regional nodes. (Book p300)

questions.q: In the Varadhachary-Katz criteria, a RESCTABLE pancreatic tumour has:
opts: No involvement of the superior mesenteric artery with a patent portal vein junction
Encasement of the superior mesenteric artery
Long segment occlusion of the portal vein
Abutment of the celiac axis of 180 degrees
questions.exp: Varadhachary-Katz: resectable (all 4 resectables), AJCC I/II — SMA no involvement, SMV/portal V junction patent — surgery. (Book p300)

questions.q: In the Varadhachary-Katz criteria, BORDERLINE pancreatic tumour has:
opts: Abutment of the superior mesenteric artery (180 degrees or less than 50%) and short segment occlusion of the portal vein junction
Encasement of the superior mesenteric artery
questions.exp: Borderline, AJCC III — SMA abutment (≥180° or <50%), celiac axis abutment, short segment occlusion of SMV/portal junction — chemotherapy then surgery. (Book p300)

questions.q: Borderline pancreatic tumours in the Varadhachary-Katz criteria are managed by:
questions.exp: Borderline: Mx — chemotherapy, then Sx. (Book p300)

questions.q: In the Varadhachary-Katz criteria, a LOCALLY ADVANCED pancreatic tumour has:
opts: Encasement of the superior mesenteric artery with long segment occlusion of the portal vein
questions.exp: Locally advanced: SMA encasement, excessive encasement of the common hepatic artery, long segment of occlusion — Mx: unresectable, palliative. (Book p300)

questions.q: The investigation of choice for peritoneal metastases in pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: Peritoneal mets: diagnostic laparoscopy — IOC. (Book p300)

questions.q: If peritoneal metastases are found at diagnostic laparoscopy, the procedure is:
questions.exp: Peritoneal mets: mets (+) — procedure abandoned. (Book p300)

questions.q: Which of the following is a criterion of unresectability in pancreatic cancer?
questions.exp: Criteria of unresectability: peritoneal mets, malignant ascites, liver mets. (Book p300)

questions.q: Which of the following is a criterion of unresectability in pancreatic cancer?
questions.exp: Criteria of unresectability: liver mets. (Book p300)

questions.q: A resectable pancreatic tumour in the HEAD (the commonest site) or periampullary is managed by:
questions.exp: Surgical management: resectable — head (m/c site), periampullary — Whipple surgery. (Book p300)

questions.q: A resectable pancreatic tumour in the BODY or TAIL is managed by:
questions.exp: Surgical management: body/tail — distal pancreatectomy. (Book p300)

questions.q: Whipple's surgery is also called:
questions.exp: Whipple surgery: pancreaticoduodenectomy. (Book p301)

questions.q: The pylorus preserving Whipple is the:
questions.exp: Pylorus preserving Whipple: Longmire transverso procedure. (Book p301)

questions.q: The pylorus preserving Whipple:
opts: Reduces the chances of dumping syndrome and is the preferred procedure
questions.exp: Pylorus preserving Whipple: decreased chances of dumping syndrome, preferred procedure. (Book p301)

questions.q: The traditional Whipple is used when:
opts: The pylorus is involved or the margin is unattainable
The tumour is in the tail
questions.exp: Pylorus preserving Whipple: involvement of pylorus/unattainable margin — traditional Whipple's. (Book p301)

questions.q: The incision for Whipple's surgery is:
questions.exp: Incision: chevron/roof top. (Book p301)

questions.q: Structures removed in Whipple's surgery include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Procedure: 1. Cholecystectomy, 2. CBD, 3. Pylorus, 4. Pancreatectomy, 5. Duodenectomy. (Book p301)

questions.q: The anastomoses performed in Whipple's surgery are:
opts: A choledochojejunostomy and a sleeve gastrostomy
questions.exp: Procedure: hepaticojejunostomy (anastomoses with common hepatic duct), gastrojejunostomy, pancreaticojejunostomy. (Book p301)

questions.q: In Whipple's surgery, the hepaticojejunostomy is made with the:
questions.exp: Anastomoses: hepaticojejunostomy — anastomoses with common hepatic duct. (Book p301)

questions.q: The tunnel of love in Whipple's surgery is:
opts: The space between the vessels and the pancreas, which needs to be intact to proceed
questions.exp: Tunnel of love: space between the vessels and pancreas; needs to be intact to proceed with Whipple's. (Book p301)

questions.q: The most common complication of Whipple's surgery is:
questions.exp: Complication: impaired gastric emptying — m/c. (Book p301)

questions.q: Impaired gastric emptying after Whipple's is due to:
questions.exp: Impaired gastric emptying: d/t loss of receptive relaxation. (Book p301)

questions.q: Impaired gastric emptying after Whipple's is more common after:
questions.exp: Impaired gastric emptying: conventional Whipple > pylorus preserving. (Book p301)

questions.q: The most common cause of death after Whipple's surgery is:
questions.exp: Complication: sepsis d/t anastomotic leak — m/c cause of death. (Book p301)

questions.q: Pancreatic fistula after Whipple's is due to:
questions.exp: Pancreatic fistula: d/t pancreaticojejunal anastomotic leak. (Book p301)

questions.q: Pancreatic fistula after Whipple's classically appears on:
opts: Post op day 2-3 with turbid, amylase-rich drainage
Immediately at the end of surgery
questions.exp: Pancreatic fistula: post op day 2-3, turbid drainage rich in amylase. (Book p301)

questions.q: Pancreatic fistula after Whipple's:
opts: Stops spontaneously and octreotide is effective
questions.exp: Pancreatic fistula: stops spontaneously; octreotide is effective. (Book p301)

questions.q: For efficacy, the better pancreatic cancer chemotherapy regimen is:
opts: Gemcitabine plus capecitabine over gemcitabine monotherapy
questions.exp: Chemotherapy: effectiveness — gemcitabine + capecitabine > gemcitabine monotherapy. (Book p301)

questions.q: For survival, the better pancreatic cancer chemotherapy regimen is:
questions.exp: Chemotherapy: survival — FOLFIRINOX > gemcitabine monotherapy. (Book p301)

questions.q: The management of an unresectable pancreatic tumour includes palliation of:
questions.exp: Management of unresectable tumour: palliation of pruritus and jaundice. (Book p301)

questions.q: Palliation of jaundice in an unresectable pancreatic tumour is done by:
questions.exp: Palliation: ERCP and stenting. (Book p301)

questions.q: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) works because:
opts: Distal blockage dilates the proximal radicals, which are punctured to drain bile
questions.exp: PTBD: distal blockage — dilatation of proximal radicals, punctured, drainage of bile. (Book p302)

questions.q: The chemotherapy listed for unresectable pancreatic tumour is:
questions.exp: Chemotherapy: NAB paclitaxel. (Book p302)

questions.q: The triple bypass palliation in an unresectable pancreatic tumour consists of:
opts: Hepaticojejunostomy, gastrojejunostomy and jejunojejunostomy, without removing the tumour
questions.exp: Palliative Sx: a. Triple bypass — hepaticojejunostomy, gastrojejunostomy, jejunojejunostomy; tumour is not removed. (Book p302)

questions.q: In the triple bypass, the gastrojejunostomy is done to:
questions.exp: Triple bypass: gastrojejunostomy — to prevent gastric outlet obstruction. (Book p302)

questions.q: In the triple bypass, the hepaticojejunostomy diverts:
questions.exp: Triple bypass: hepaticojejunostomy — bile to jejunum. (Book p302)

questions.q: Palliative coeliac ganglion block in pancreatic cancer is done to:
questions.exp: Palliative Sx: b. Coeliac ganglion block — decreases pain. (Book p302)

questions.q: The most important prognostic factor in pancreatic cancer is:
questions.exp: Prognostic factor: stage (most important). (Book p302)

questions.q: The most common endocrine tumour of the pancreas is:
questions.exp: Insulinoma: m/c endocrine tumour. (Book p302)

questions.q: Insulinoma arises from:
questions.exp: Insulinoma: arises from beta-cells. (Book p302)

questions.q: What proportion of insulinomas are benign?
questions.exp: Insulinoma: 90% benign. (Book p302)

questions.q: Insulinomas are distributed in the pancreas:
questions.exp: Insulinoma: evenly distributed throughout. (Book p302)

questions.q: Whipple's triad in insulinoma consists of:
opts: Fasting hypoglycaemia, a low blood glucose value (less than 50 mg/dL) and rapid resolution on giving glucose
questions.exp: Whipple's triad: fasting hypoglycaemia, low blood glucose value (<50 mg/dL), rapid resolution on giving glucose. (Book p302)

questions.q: In Whipple's triad, the blood glucose value is:
questions.exp: Whipple's triad: low blood glucose value (<50 mg/dL). (Book p302)

questions.q: The gold standard test for insulinoma is:
questions.exp: Investigation: gold standard test — 72 hrs fasting test; obsolete. (Book p302)

questions.q: In insulinoma, the insulin to glucose ratio is:
questions.exp: Investigation: insulin/glucose >0.3. (Book p302)

questions.q: The best method of localisation of an insulinoma is:
questions.exp: Investigation: best method of localisation — endoscopic ultrasound. (Book p302)

questions.q: Compared with exogenous insulin injection, an insulinoma shows:
questions.exp: Table: conditions with raised fasting insulin — exogenous insulin injections have a normal C peptide; insulinoma has a raised C peptide. (Book p302)

questions.q: An insulinoma GREATER than 2 cm is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: >2 cm — wider resection. (Book p303)

questions.q: An insulinoma LESS than 2 cm is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: <2 cm — enucleation. (Book p303)

questions.q: Diazoxide in insulinoma:
opts: Inhibits insulin release and prevents hypoglycaemia
questions.exp: Management: diazoxide — inhibits release of insulin and prevents hypoglycaemia. (Book p303)

questions.q: Insulinoma with metastasis is treated with:
questions.exp: Management: in metastasis — chemotherapy, streptozocin, diazoxide. (Book p303)

questions.q: Gastrinoma is also known as:
questions.exp: Gastrinoma: aka Zollinger Ellison syndrome. (Book p303)

questions.q: Gastrinoma arises from:
questions.exp: Gastrinoma: arise from gastrin producing (G-cells) cells. (Book p303)

questions.q: Gastrinoma is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm in:
questions.exp: Gastrinoma: m/c pancreatic endocrine neoplasm in MEN 1 syndrome. (Book p303)

questions.q: What proportion of gastrinomas are malignant?
questions.exp: Gastrinoma: malignant (70-80%). (Book p303)

questions.q: Passaro's (gastrinoma) triangle is:
opts: The most common site of the gastrinoma
The site of the cystic artery
questions.exp: Passaro's triangle/gastrinoma triangle: m/c site of the gastrinoma. (Book p303)

questions.q: One boundary of Passaro's triangle is:
opts: The junction of the cystic and common hepatic duct
questions.exp: Boundaries: junction of cystic + common hepatic duct. (Book p303)

questions.q: Another boundary of Passaro's triangle is:
opts: The junction of the head and neck with the body of the pancreas
questions.exp: Boundaries: junction of head and neck with body of the pancreas. (Book p303)

questions.q: The third boundary of Passaro's triangle is:
opts: The junction of D2 and D3 of the duodenum
questions.exp: Boundaries: junction of D2 and D3 (D: duodenum). (Book p303)

questions.q: The most common site of a gastrinoma is the wall of:
questions.exp: M/c site of gastrinoma: wall of D1. (Book p303)

questions.q: A gastrinoma located OUTSIDE Passaro's triangle is:
opts: More aggressive, larger in size, with poor prognosis
questions.exp: Gastrinoma outside Passaro's triangle: more aggressive, larger in size, poor prognosis. (Book p303)

questions.q: The clinical features of gastrinoma include:
opts: Pain, diarrhoea, multiple recurrent peptic ulcers
questions.exp: Clinical features: pain, diarrhoea, peptic ulcer, multiple, recurrent. (Book p303)

questions.q: Atypical locations of gastrinoma peptic ulcers include:
questions.exp: Clinical features: atypical locations — D3, jejunum. (Book p303)

questions.q: In gastrinoma, the diarrhoea is due to:
opts: Acidic pH in the duodenum causing non-activation of pancreatic enzymes and malabsorption
questions.exp: Pathophysiology: raised gastrin — raised HCl production, peptic ulcer; acidic pH in duodenum — non-activation pancreatic enzyme, malabsorption and diarrhoea. (Book p303)

questions.q: The Zollinger Ellison triad consists of:
opts: Increased gastrin, increased acid output and a non-beta cell tumour
Fasting hypoglycaemia, low glucose and resolution on glucose
questions.exp: Zollinger Ellison triad: 1. Increased gastrin, 2. Increased acid output, 3. Non-beta cell tumour. (Book p304)

questions.q: A serum gastrin level greater than 1000 pg/mL in gastrinoma is:
questions.exp: Diagnosis: S. gastrin >1000 pg/mL — diagnostic. (Book p304)

questions.q: When the serum gastrin is less than 1000 pg/mL, the secretin stimulation test is positive if:
opts: Serum gastrin rises by 300 pg/mL after the test
questions.exp: Diagnosis: S. gastrin <1000 pg/mL — secretin stimulation test, S. gastrin increased by 300 pg/mL after test — positive. (Book p304)

questions.q: A pH of less than 2.0 in the duodenum is:
opts: Seen only in Zollinger Ellison triad patients with no treatment
questions.exp: Diagnosis: pH <2.0 — diagnostic. (Book p304)

questions.q: For localisation, gastrinoma is investigated by SRS, which stands for:
questions.exp: Localisation: SRS — somatostatin receptor scintigraphy. (Book p304)

questions.q: On somatostatin receptor scintigraphy, a gastrinoma:
questions.exp: SRS: does not lighten — insulinoma; lightens — gastrinoma. (Book p304)

questions.q: On somatostatin receptor scintigraphy, an insulinoma:
questions.exp: SRS: does not lighten — insulinoma. (Book p304)

questions.q: A patient with gastrinoma should also be evaluated for:
questions.exp: Localisation: evaluation for MEN 1 syndrome. (Book p304)

questions.q: A gastrinoma GREATER than 5 mm is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: >5 mm — full thickness resection. (Book p304)

questions.q: A gastrinoma of 5 mm or LESS is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: <5 mm — enucleation. (Book p304)

questions.q: The most common site of gastrinoma metastasis is:
questions.exp: Metastasis: m/c site — liver. (Book p304)

questions.q: Octreotide in gastrinoma is used to:
questions.exp: Metastasis: octreotide — decreased secretion of gastrin. (Book p304)

questions.q: Streptozocin is used in gastrinoma for:
questions.exp: Metastasis: streptozocin — for malignant/metastatic carcinoma. (Book p304)

questions.q: Glucagonoma arises from:
opts: Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.exp: Glucagonoma: origin — alpha cells of islets of Langerhans. (Book p304)

questions.q: Diabetes in glucagonoma is due to:
questions.exp: Glucagonoma: diabetes — d/t raised blood sugar. (Book p304)

questions.q: The dermatitis of glucagonoma is:
questions.exp: Glucagonoma: dermatitis — necrolytic migratory rash. (Book p304)

questions.q: Migratory thrombophlebitis in glucagonoma is also known as:
questions.exp: Glucagonoma: DVT — migratory thrombophlebitis — Trousseau syndrome. (Book p304)

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of glucagonoma?
questions.exp: Glucagonoma: depression. (Book p304)

questions.q: WDHA syndrome is also known as:
questions.exp: WDHA syndrome: aka Verner Morrison syndrome. (Book p305)

questions.q: WDHA syndrome is due to a raised:
questions.exp: WDHA syndrome: d/t raised vasoactive intestinal peptide — VIPoma. (Book p305)

questions.q: The features of WDHA syndrome include:
opts: Watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria and acidosis
questions.exp: WDHA: watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria, acidosis. (Book p305)

questions.q: The features of somatostatinoma include:
opts: Steatorrhoea due to malabsorption, diabetes and cholelithiasis
questions.exp: Somatostatinoma: steatorrhoea d/t malabsorption, diabetes, cholelithiasis. (Book p305)

questions.q: A non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm is typically seen in:
questions.exp: Non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm: elderly patients. (Book p305)

questions.q: A non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm is usually:
questions.exp: Non functional: malignant. (Book p305)

questions.q: The most common site of origin of a non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm is:
questions.exp: Non functional: origin — m/c head of pancreas. (Book p305)

questions.q: Blood markers of a non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm include:
questions.exp: Non functional: presence of chromogranin A, synaptophysin in blood. (Book p305)

questions.q: The management of a non functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasm is:
questions.exp: Non functional: Mx — resection. (Book p305)

questions.q: A serous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas is most commonly sited at:
questions.exp: Serous cystic neoplasm: site — head of pancreas (m/c). (Book p305)

questions.q: Serous cystic neoplasms are seen in:
questions.exp: Serous cystic neoplasm: older patients. (Book p305)

questions.q: Serous cystic neoplasms are characterised histologically by:
questions.exp: Serous cystic neoplasm: presence of glycogen rich cells. (Book p305)

questions.q: In a serous cystic neoplasm, the CEA is:
questions.exp: Serous cystic neoplasm: CEA not raised; large multiloculate mass, usually benign. (Book p305)

questions.q: A serous cystic neoplasm on CECT shows:
questions.exp: Investigation: CECT (IOC) — sunburst appearance. (Book p305)

questions.q: A large and symptomatic serous cystic neoplasm is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: large and symptomatic — enucleation. (Book p305)

questions.q: A small and asymptomatic serous cystic neoplasm is managed by:
questions.exp: Management: small and asymptomatic — observation. (Book p305)

questions.q: Mucinous tumours of the pancreas are most commonly sited at:
opts: The body and tail of the pancreas
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: site — body and tail of pancreas. (Book p306)

questions.q: Mucinous cystic neoplasms are most common in:
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: m/c in females (pre menopausal). (Book p306)

questions.q: The characteristic stroma of a mucinous cystic neoplasm is:
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: ovarian like stroma. (Book p306)

questions.q: Mucinous cystic neoplasms are:
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: ER, PR +ve. (Book p306)

questions.q: The CEA in a mucinous tumour of the pancreas is:
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: raised CEA. (Book p306)

questions.q: A history of pancreatitis is a feature of a mucinous tumour, and the differential diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Mucinous tumours: H/o pancreatitis (+); D/d — pseudocyst. (Book p306)

questions.q: Compared with a mucinous tumour, a pseudocyst is:
questions.exp: Note: pseudocyst — homogenous, CEA not elevated. (Book p306)

units.title: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN
units.sec: Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: Risk Factors and PanIN · p297
units.guide: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is the commonest carcinoma of the pancreas, fed by smoking, obesity, African American ethnicity, chronic pancreatitis and the gene list — PRSS1 of hereditary pancreatitis, SPINK1 of tropical calcific pancreatitis — plus the syndromes: Peutz-Jeghers (STK11) with its 100-fold risk, the melanoma-mole family, cystic fibrosis, BRCA-2 (pancreas, prostate, male breast), Lynch (and its colorectal risk) and FAP. The road runs through PanIN: K-ras first and commonest at 1A/1B, CDKN2A at 2A, p53 and SMAD4 at 3, then the final hit — K53.

units.title: Periampullary Carcinoma and Courvoisier's Law
units.sec: Periampullary Carcinoma and Courvoisier's Law · p298
units.guide: Periampullary carcinoma bundles four cancers within 2 cm of the ampulla — pancreatic head, ampullary, distal cholangiocarcinoma and duodenal adenocarcinoma — with similar presentation and management. They present as progressive, surgical obstructive jaundice with weight loss, and pain that bites hardest from the body and tail. The ampullary variety waxes and wanes, each fade of jaundice sloughing tumour into the bowel as melena; the duodenal adenocarcinoma blocks the outlet. Courvoisier's law holds firm — a palpable gallbladder with obstructive jaundice is seldom stone, because stones fibrose the gallbladder shrivelled while a tumour lets it balloon pyriform and palpable; the exceptions are the 10% primary CBD stone, double impaction, the Chinese liver fluke of oriental cholangiohepatitis and Mirizzi's fistula.

units.title: Investigation of Pancreatic Cancer
units.guide: CECT is the IOC of pancreatic cancer; duodenography with its Frostberg reverse 3 sign is obsolete, and the X-ray shows only widened duodenal loops. MRCP and ERCP carry the double duct sign — a blocked ampulla dilating both the pancreatic duct and the CBD — and when the radiological diagnosis is in doubt, a transgastric EUS-guided FNAC settles it. CA 19-9 is the predictive and prognostic marker that flags patients for staging laparoscopy before definitive surgery, stays an important (if not specific) prognostic marker when normalised by neoadjuvant chemo, and is shared with cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer; PET CT completes the staging.

units.title: Staging and Resectability
units.guide: The AJCC stages it: T1 up to 2 cm, T2 from 2 to 4, T3 beyond 4, T4 by adjacent involvement; M1 metastases land in the liver; N1 is 1-3 nodes, N2 more than three. Varadhachary-Katz decides resectability on the vessels — a clear SMA with a patent portal junction goes straight to surgery; abutment over 180 degrees or under 50% with short-segment occlusion is borderline, taking chemotherapy before surgery; encasement with long-segment occlusion is locally advanced and palliative. Diagnostic laparoscopy is the IOC for peritoneal mets — found, and the procedure is abandoned; peritoneal mets, malignant ascites or liver mets write the word unresectable. Resectable head or periampullary disease is Whipple's; body and tail take a distal pancreatectomy.

units.title: Whipple's Surgery
units.guide: Whipple's is the pancreaticoduodenectomy: a chevron or roof top incision, then cholecystectomy, CBD, pylorus, pancreatectomy and duodenectomy out, and three anastomoses in — hepaticojejunostomy on the common hepatic duct, gastrojejunostomy and pancreaticojejunostomy. The pylorus-preserving Longmire transverso variant is preferred for fewer dumping syndrome episodes, with the conventional Whipple reserved for an involved pylorus or unattainable margin; the tunnel of love between vessels and pancreas must be intact to proceed at all. Its complications rank: impaired gastric emptying is the commonest (lost receptive relaxation, worse with the conventional), sepsis from anastomotic leak the commonest cause of death, and the pancreatic fistula — a pancreaticojejunostomy leak on post op day 2-3 with turbid amylase-rich drainage that stops spontaneously and answers to octreotide. Gemcitabine plus capecitabine beats monotherapy for effect, FOLFIRINOX for survival.

units.title: Management of Unresectable Tumour
units.guide: Unresectable disease is palliated: the pruritus and jaundice by ERCP stenting or PTBD (the distal blockage dilates the proximal radicals for puncture drainage), pain by coeliac ganglion block, and the double obstruction prophylactically by the triple bypass — hepaticojejunostomy for bile, gastrojejunostomy against gastric outlet obstruction, jejunojejunostomy — all without touching the tumour. NAB paclitaxel is the listed chemo, and stage remains the most important prognostic factor.

units.title: Insulinoma
units.guide: The insulinoma is the commonest endocrine tumour, a beta-cell lesion, 90% benign and evenly scattered through the gland. Whipple's triad — fasting hypoglycaemia, glucose below 50, rapid resolution with glucose — frames it; the 72-hour fast was the gold standard until it went obsolete, and now the insulin/glucose ratio over 0.3 and the C peptide (raised, unlike exogenous insulin's normal one) carry the diagnosis, with EUS as the best localisation. Under 2 cm it is enucleated, over 2 cm more widely resected; diazoxide holds the insulin in check, and metastatic disease takes chemotherapy, streptozocin and diazoxide.

units.title: Gastrinoma
units.guide: The gastrinoma — Zollinger Ellison syndrome — is the G-cell tumour, the commonest pancreatic endocrine neoplasm of MEN 1, malignant in 70-80%. It hides in Passaro's triangle (cystic-common hepatic junction, head-neck to body junction, D2-D3 junction), most often in the wall of D1; outside the triangle it is bigger, more aggressive and poorer. Acid floods: gastrin up, HCl up, ulcers multiple, recurrent and atypical in D3 and jejunum, the acidic duodenum inactivating the enzymes into malabsorptive diarrhoea. The triad — raised gastrin, raised acid output, non-beta cell tumour — is proved by a gastrin above 1000, or a secretin rise of 300 below that, with a duodenal pH under 2. SRS lights it up (the insulinoma stays dark), MEN 1 is screened, over 5 mm is fully resected, under 5 mm enucleated, and liver metastases take octreotide against the gastrin and streptozocin against the malignancy.

units.title: Glucagonoma, WDHA and Somatostatinoma
units.guide: The rare endocrines each keep their signature: the glucagonoma from alpha cells brings diabetes from high sugar, the necrolytic migratory rash, migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau) and depression. WDHA — Verner Morrison — is the VIPoma of watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria and acidosis; the somatostatinoma steatorrhoeas, sweetens the blood to diabetes and seeds the gallbladder with stones.

units.title: Non-functional and Cystic Neoplasms
units.guide: The non-functional endocrine neoplasm hits the elderly, is malignant, favours the head and announces itself with chromogranin A and synaptophysin — resect it. The cystic neoplasms are a family to sort: the serous cystic neoplasm, an older patient's head mass of glycogen-rich cells, CEA normal, multiloculated and usually benign, sunburst on CECT — enucleated if large and symptomatic, watched if small. The mucinous tumour, pre-menopausal women in the body and tail with ovarian-like stroma, ER/PR positive, CEA raised and a pancreatitis history (against which the pseudocyst is homogeneous and CEA quiet), egg-shell calcified with a heterogeneous lining. IPMN comes in branch, main and mixed (branch first, then main), triad of Ohashi — dilated hepatopancreatic duct, fish-mouth ampulla, mucin oozing — diagnosed by ERCP: main/mixed over 2 cm resected, branch duct up to 2 cm observed. And the solid pseudopapillary (Gruber Frantz, aka Hamoudi) tumour of the tail in women, beta-catenin/vimentin mutated, is resected.
